_comment: Backstory starts (scripts/sim/backstories.gd Backstories; DESIGN_LIVING_WORLD.md): the New Company screen offers a start at each of a company type's recommended ports (data/starts.json, type_starts.json, the Great Lakes), each an archetype from this list picked by the port (the same every game) and told in three or four sentences assembled from these parts. A start sets the money, any debt (a loan to repay) or investors (a stake in the company, held by the backers named), the ships the company begins with (by the type's first-tier models: first = the cheapest, second = the next; condition = maintenance 0 to 1, age_hours = hours at sea already), the standing with countries and firms (relations: home = the home country, neighbours = the countries round it, firm = the biggest firm based in the home country; to be used when reputation arrives) and the CEO's traits (data/traits.json; picked from `traits`, `traits_count` of them). The player can also take a custom start (Backstories.custom()). Amounts in US$; money and debt are scaled a little by the port's kind (kind_money: an excellent port's story is poorer, a hard one's richer, so starts even out). Template words: {ceo} the CEO's name (the full name the first time it appears, the first name after), {surname} the family name, {port} the home port, {country} its country, {money}, {debt}, {stake}, {ship} the first ship's name and {ships} all of them, {backer} the investors' name, {firm} the firm, {trait} the first trait's story line.

archetypes.name: The inheritance
story: {ceo} grew up on the quays of {port}, where the family ran one old ship for forty years.
When the old man died the ship, {ship}, came to {ceo} with {money} in the bank and a lifetime of debts to nobody.
She's worn and slow, but she's paid for.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The commander's pension
story: {ceo} spent twenty-two years in the {country} navy and left it a commander, with a pension, a lump sum and no wish to sit still.
{money} is what the lump sum and the house came to, and {port} is where the ships are.
The old service has long arms, and {ceo} still knows people in every harbour office at home.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The lucky ticket
story: {ceo} was a deckhand at {port} with a ticket in a back pocket and the numbers came up.
After the tax and the family there was {money} left, and {ceo} had always wanted to own the ship rather than scrub it.
Nobody at the port quite believes it yet.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The backers
story: {ceo} pitched a shipping line out of {port} to {backer} and they bought it.
They put up {money} for {stake} of the company, and they will want to see returns.
The money is real, the strings are too.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The mortgage
story: {ceo} walked into a bank in {port} with a business plan and walked out with {money}.
{debt} of it is the bank's, at interest, and the bank will want it back whether the ships sail or not.
The plan is good; it had better be.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The payout
story: {ceo} ran operations for {firm} out of {port} until the merger made the job disappear.
The settlement came to {money}, and {ceo} knows exactly which cargoes the old firm leaves on the quay.
They will not be pleased to see a former manager across the table.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The auction lot
story: Two ships came up at a creditors' auction in {port} and {ceo} was the only bidder who had seen their engine rooms.
{ships} went for scrap money, and {money} is what was left over to run them.
They need work, all of it overdue.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The family firm
story: The {surname} family has shipped out of {port} for three generations, and now it is {ceo}'s turn.
The firm comes with {ship}, {money} in the accounts and a name every broker in {country} knows.
Expectations come with it too.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The foreign partner
story: A trading house abroad wanted a foothold in {port} and {ceo} was the local partner it found.
{money} came with the deal, and {stake} of the company went the other way.
Half the decisions will be argued over a bad phone line.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The savings
story: {ceo} kept the books for half the shipping offices in {port} and saved for twenty years.
{money} is every cent of it, and this is the one chance it buys.
There is no second savings account.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The breaker's yard
story: {ceo} ran a ship-breaking yard outside {port} and one day kept a ship instead of cutting it.
{ship} is bigger than a new company has any right to, and worn to match; {money} came from selling the yard.
What breaks, {ceo} can fix.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The captain comes ashore
story: Thirty years in command, the last ten saving, and {ceo} bought {ship} outright and came ashore to run her.
{money} is left for fuel, crew and the first cargo out of {port}.
The crew know the new owner has stood every watch they have.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The founders' round
story: {ceo} sold a fund on a smarter kind of shipping company, run from {port} on data and nerve.
The round raised {money} for {stake} of the company.
The spreadsheet is beautiful; the sea has not read it.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The co-operative
story: The dockers of {port} pooled what they had and asked {ceo} to run a line of their own.
{money} of hard-earned money sits in the account, and every one of them is watching it.
No crew will ever work harder for a boss.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The partner's share
story: {ceo}'s late partner held a quarter of {firm}, and the firm bought the share back in ships and cash rather than see it sold on.
{ship} and {money} were the settlement, delivered at {port} with a handshake.
The old firm still calls to ask how things are.
{trait}

archetypes.name: The quiet fortune
story: Nobody in {port} asks where {ceo}'s {money} came from, and {ceo} does not say.
The customs house has a file, and the file has nothing in it that would stand up.
A proper shipping line would make a very respectable front.
{trait}
